note: Authored City Watch street cases from the docs/cases briefs (CW-NC-05, CW-NC-08, CW-NC-12, CW-NC-43), plus the old engine's 14 street cases (CW-SC-01 to 14) and its Thirteenth Chime mystery (CW-MY-01), ported to the current city. CW-NC-01 The Bridge That Was Closed is the team's pilot in cases/bridge-closure.mjs, offered from Duty. Original stories; unnamed witnesses are invented residents, not canon.

bridge.name: the Watch-side approach to Pon’s Bridge

quay.name: the quay by the Dock Warehouse

crypthouse.name: a house by the Old Crypt

opera.name: the gutter outside the Opera House

outpost.name: the corner by the Watch Outpost

butchers.name: the collection yard by the Butchers’ Guild

cases.title: A Receipt for a Raincoat
cases.where: the Market and the Mended Drum
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Gentleman says his raincoat’s on a stall by the Market Hall, and the stallholder’s got a receipt for it. Now, I’m not saying anyone’s lying. I’m saying someone’s wrong, and I’d like it to be someone who isn’t me.”
cases.brief: Find out whose coat it is, and how a receipt came to be with it. Get the coat home without accusing anyone you can’t prove did wrong.

clues.seam: The coat on the stall has a little anchor darned into the collar, exactly as the owner described. It is his coat.
clues.receipt: The stallholder’s receipt is genuine, from a pawnshop, but it describes a coat with brass buttons and a hood. This coat has horn buttons and no hood.
clues.mixup: At the Mended Drum, two coats hung on one peg. A customer took the wrong one home, then sold it with the receipt for his own coat. The stallholder bought it honestly.

scenes.label: Examine the raincoat
scenes.title: A raincoat on a stall
scenes.text: A sturdy oilskin raincoat, much loved and much mended. Inside the collar someone has darned a tiny anchor in thick thread, just as the owner said.

scenes.label: Read the stallholder’s receipt
scenes.title: The stallholder’s receipt
scenes.speaker: The stallholder
scenes.text: “Bought fair and square, I did. Here’s the receipt.” The receipt is real enough. It describes a raincoat with brass buttons and a hood. The coat in front of you has horn buttons and nowhere to keep a hood.

scenes.label: Decide how to handle the coat
scenes.title: The coat and the receipt
scenes.speaker: The stallholder
scenes.text: “If it’s his coat, it’s his coat. But I paid for it, and I don’t like being called a thief.”

choice.prompt: You can settle this now, or dig into how the wrong receipt got here.

options.label: Arrange the return now, no accusations
options.text: You agree the coat goes home, and promise the stallholder the receipt question will be looked into. Nobody is called a thief. Everybody is slightly damp.

options.label: Find out how the wrong receipt got here
options.text: The stallholder remembers where it came from: “Bloke from the Mended Drum sold it me. Said he had the receipt to prove it was his.”

scenes.label: Ask about the coat at the Mended Drum
scenes.title: Coats at the Mended Drum
scenes.speaker: A regular by the door
scenes.text: “Peg by the door only takes one coat, so people hang two. Last wet night, two raincoats, one peg. Fellow grabbed the wrong one going home, sold it the next day with his own receipt, thinking it was his. Came back this morning looking for his real one, very embarrassed.”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting the raincoat
file.prompt: “Right then. Whose coat is it, and is anybody going in the cells?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: The stallholder stole the coat
findings.reject: “The stallholder paid for it and kept the receipt,” says Colon. “That’s not theft. That’s bad luck with paperwork.”

findings.label: It’s the owner’s coat: returned, nobody blamed
findings.summary: Coat returned; how the receipt got there was left open.
findings.reply: “Coat goes home, nobody gets accused of anything they didn’t do,” says Colon. “Proper policing, that. The receipt business can stay a mystery. The city’s full of them.”

findings.label: An honest mix-up at the Mended Drum: wrong coat, wrong receipt
findings.summary: Honest mix-up explained; coat returned, nobody to blame.
findings.reply: “Two coats, one peg,” says Colon, delighted. “Nobody’s a criminal, everybody gets their own coat back, and I get to write ‘peg-related’ on a form. Best kind of case.”

cases.title: The Fine on the Nail
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “People in the Shades are finding fines nailed to their doors. Watch fines, supposedly. Thing is, we don’t do fines by nail. We don’t hardly do fines at all, it’s all the writing.”
cases.brief: Check whether the fines are real, find out if anyone has actually paid, and stop people being cheated. You never pay anything yourself.

clues.notice: The notice nailed in the Shades says ‘FINE: 3 coins for Unlicensed Washing. Pay the collector. By order of the Watch.’ No signature, no number.
clues.norecord: The duty desk has no fines for washing, no collector, and no record of any notices in the Shades. The Watch never issued them.
clues.paid: A neighbour paid 3 coins to a man in a long coat who said he was collecting for the Watch. Money was really taken.
clues.collector: You watched the collector make his rounds and saw him take another payment. You can describe him and where he goes.

scenes.label: Read the notice on the nail
scenes.title: A fine on a nail
scenes.text: FINE: 3 COINS FOR UNLICENSED WASHING. PAY THE COLLECTOR. BY ORDER OF THE WATCH. It is nailed to a door that has clearly not been washed, licensed or otherwise, in years.

scenes.label: Check the duty desk records
scenes.title: The duty desk
scenes.speaker: The desk officer
scenes.text: “Fines for washing? In the Shades? We’d be more likely to give out medals for it.” The ledger has no such fine, no collector, and nothing about the Shades but the usual.

scenes.label: Decide what to tell the residents
scenes.title: Warn them, or watch first?
scenes.speaker: A resident
scenes.text: “So it’s not real? Then who’s been coming round for the money?”

choice.prompt: Warning everyone now stops anyone else paying. Keeping quiet a little longer might show you who is collecting.

options.label: Warn the street now: nobody pays
options.text: Word travels down the street faster than you can walk it. Nobody else will be paying any fines today. Somebody mentions a neighbour by the Market who already paid.

options.label: Say nothing yet and watch for the collector
options.text: You ask the resident to keep this between you for an hour. They agree, with the expression of someone who will tell everyone in an hour and five minutes. The collector works the Market side next, they say.

scenes.label: Talk to the neighbour who paid
scenes.title: The neighbour who paid
scenes.speaker: A neighbour
scenes.text: “Three coins, I gave him. Long coat, very polite, said it was for the Watch. I thought, well, at least it’s not for the Thieves’ Guild. Should I have thought harder?”

scenes.label: Watch the collector make his rounds
scenes.title: Watching the collector
scenes.text: A man in a long coat works along the Market side, tapping each notice and holding out his hand. A woman pays him three coins. You note his face, his coat and where he goes next. Then you warn the street, so nobody else pays.

file.label: Report to Captain Carrot
file.title: Reporting the fines
file.prompt: “Are these fines real? And if not, has anybody been cheated?”
file.reject: Carrot shakes his head gently. “Your notes don’t say that yet. What do you actually know?”

findings.label: The fines are real, so residents should pay
findings.reject: “No signature, no record at the desk,” says Carrot. “The Watch doesn’t fine people by nail.”

findings.label: False notices: no such fine exists
findings.summary: Notices shown to be fake; no one proven to have been cheated.
findings.reply: “Good,” says Carrot. “Fake notices are a nuisance, and you’ve shown they’re fake. If anyone was actually paid, we’ll need a witness to prove it.”

findings.label: Fraud: money was taken for a fake fine
findings.summary: Fraud proven: money was taken for fake fines.

replies.warn: “You warned them first and still found the proof,” says Carrot. “Nobody else paid today because of you. We don’t know the collector’s face yet, but we know what he did.”

findings.reply: “The notice was fake and somebody paid,” says Carrot. “That’s fraud, and it’s proven.”

findings.label: Fraud by the collector you watched
findings.summary: Collector seen taking money; fraud proven and he can be found.
findings.reply: “Fake fine, a payment you saw, and a description good enough to find him,” says Carrot. “And you warned the street once you had it. That’s the job done properly.”

cases.title: The Bread at the Wrong Door
cases.where: the docks, Crust Hall and Netmender’s Shack
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “The dock crews’ bread came short again. Four sacks ordered, the warehouse says they got three and a bit, and the porters are saying the bakers are diddling them. Bakers say they never short anyone. Somebody’s wrong, and the porters are getting peckish, which is never good for public order.”
cases.brief: Find out where the missing bread went. A Crust Hall wrapper on a sack doesn’t prove the bakers did anything wrong, so don’t blame them unless you can show it.

clues.wrapper: The sacks at the quay are Crust Hall’s: the guild’s wheatsheaf is stamped on every one.
clues.count: The sacks at the quay hold seven loaves each and are folded over once at the neck.
clues.tally: Crust Hall’s tally says four sacks of ten loaves, each folded twice and tucked, the guild’s way. Forty loaves left the bakery.
clues.counted: A dock clerk watched you count the bread: twenty-eight loaves in four sacks, all signed for on the tally sheet.
clues.switch: The net-mender saw a man lift four sacks off the bread cart behind the warehouse, leave four lighter sacks in their place, and walk off towards the Shades with the full ones.

scenes.label: Look at the bread sacks
scenes.title: Bread sacks on the quay
scenes.speaker: A porter
scenes.text: “There. Bakers’ sacks, see? Their mark on every one.” The wheatsheaf of the Bakers’ Guild is stamped on all four sacks. The porter folds his arms like a man who has proved something.

scenes.label: Count the loaves in the sacks
scenes.title: Counting the bread
scenes.text: Seven loaves in the first sack. Seven in the second, seven in the third, seven in the fourth. Each sack is folded over once at the neck and tied with dock string.

scenes.label: Ask Crust Hall about the dock order
scenes.title: The bakers’ tally
scenes.speaker: A flour-dusted baker
scenes.text: “Forty loaves. Four sacks of ten, same as every week.” She shows you the tally, signed by the carter. “And we fold the neck twice and tuck it, so it travels. We’ve folded it like that since before the Guild had a hall. Anyone who folds once isn’t us.”

scenes.label: Decide what to do with the bread
scenes.title: Hungry porters
scenes.speaker: The porter
scenes.text: “Are we eating this or not? The tide won’t wait and neither will my stomach.”

choice.prompt: You can hand the bread out now, or get a proper count witnessed first.

options.label: Hand out the bread now
options.text: The porters cheer, the bread goes, and the sacks go into the river barrel. Good for morale. Bad for evidence.

options.label: Have the dock clerk witness a count first
options.text: The dock clerk grumbles, counts with you, and signs the tally sheet. Then the porters eat. It takes ten minutes and earns you several dark looks.

scenes.label: Ask the net-mender what she saw
scenes.title: Behind the warehouse
scenes.speaker: The net-mender
scenes.text: “Bread cart? Stood behind the warehouse half the morning, nobody watching it. Fellow came along with four sacks on a barrow, swapped them for the four on the cart, cool as you like, and wheeled the full ones off towards the Shades. Thought he was a baker. Didn’t fold anything, mind. Just swapped.”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting the bread
file.prompt: “Well? Are the bakers robbing the docks, or are the docks just hungry?”
file.reject: Colon reads your notes twice. “That’s not what this says. Have another look.”

findings.label: Crust Hall short-delivered the bread
findings.reject: “Their sacks, yes,” says Colon. “But anyone can carry a sack. You’d need more than a wheatsheaf to say the bakers did it, and the Bakers’ Guild has very good lawyers. And very good buns.”

findings.label: The bread came short, but not from the bakery
findings.summary: Bakers cleared; where the bread went was left open.
findings.reply: “Forty went out, twenty-eight turned up, and the sacks are folded wrong,” says Colon. “So it’s not the bakers. Good. I’ll tell the porters to stop glaring at people with flour on them. Where the rest went, well. Somewhere with very full stomachs.”
findings.reject: “You’ll want what the bakers sent and what turned up,” says Colon. “Can’t say it came short till you know both numbers.”

findings.label: Someone swapped the sacks on the cart after delivery; the bakers are not to blame
findings.summary: Sacks switched on the cart after delivery; witnessed count and witness statement filed; bakers cleared.
findings.reply: “A witnessed count, the bakers’ tally and somebody who saw the swap,” says Colon, impressed despite himself. “That’s a report. Bakers cleared, and next week the cart doesn’t stand about unwatched behind the warehouse. I’ll put someone on it. Not me. I’m allergic to fish.”
findings.reject: “For that I need two things,” says Colon. “A count somebody official watched you make, and a witness who saw where the bread went. Bread gets eaten. Stories get bigger. Paper stays the same size.”

cases.title: The Sack With Two Tags
cases.where: the quay, the Post Office, the Bonded warehouse and Netmender’s Shack
cases.giverLine: Captain Carrot: “There’s a mail sack sitting on the quay that nobody will touch. It has two tags on it, and they say two different places. The dock clerk won’t pass it on until someone works out which one is right. It’s probably only a muddle. But a muddle with a sack in it can turn into a theft very quickly, so I’d like it settled properly.”
cases.brief: Find out which tag on the sack is the real one, and how the second tag got there. Don’t open the sack, and don’t blame anyone you can’t tie to the swap.

clues.tags: The sack on the quay has two tags. A new routing tag says “Bonded warehouse, the Shades”. An old, curled return label says “Return to the Post Office”.
clues.dispatch: At the Post Office, the clerk shows that the dispatch stamp is pressed half over the routing tag. The return label is stuck on top of the stamp, so it went on after the sack left the Post Office.
clues.expected: The Bonded warehouse clerk has the sack in his bond book, due today, under the same number as the routing tag.
clues.held: The sack is held unopened at the quay office, with the dock clerk as witness, until the record is checked.
clues.switch: The net-mender saw the carter’s mate in the red cap paste an old label onto the sack on the quay steps, while the carter was round the back with the horse.

scenes.label: Look at the mail sack
scenes.title: A sack nobody will touch
scenes.speaker: The dock clerk
scenes.text: “Two tags, officer, and they don’t agree.” The sack is sealed and heavy. A crisp routing tag says Bonded warehouse, the Shades. Under it, tied on with different string, an old curled label says Return to the Post Office. “I pass it on to the wrong one, and it’s my name in the book.”

scenes.label: Ask at the Post Office about the sack
scenes.title: The dispatch stamp
scenes.speaker: A Post Office clerk
scenes.text: The clerk finds the entry at once. “Sent out this morning, to the Bonded warehouse. Look at the stamp: it’s pressed half over the routing tag, the way we always do.” She taps the return label. “That one’s an old label from some other journey, and it’s stuck right on top of our stamp. Whoever put it on, it wasn’t us. It went on after the sack left here.”

scenes.label: Ask the Bonded warehouse whether they expect a sack
scenes.title: The bond book
scenes.speaker: The warehouse clerk
scenes.text: The clerk runs a finger down his bond book. “Here. One sack from the Post Office, due today, same number as that tag. It hasn’t come.” He frowns. “Duty’s already paid on it, so there’s no reason for anyone to send it back.”

scenes.label: Decide what to do with the sack
scenes.title: The waiting sack
scenes.speaker: The dock clerk
scenes.text: “So what do I do with it? I can’t stand here guarding a sack all day.”

choice.prompt: You can send the sack back to the Post Office unopened, or keep it here under a witness while the record is checked.

options.label: Send it back to the Post Office unopened
options.text: A runner takes the sack back up to the Post Office. It’s safe there, and the quay is clear. But the sack is no longer where the swap happened.

options.label: Keep it at the quay office under a witness
options.text: The dock clerk locks the sack in the quay office and writes the time in his book, with your name beside it. Nobody opens it.

scenes.label: Ask the net-mender whether she saw the sack
scenes.title: On the quay steps
scenes.speaker: The net-mender
scenes.text: “That sack? Came down on the mail cart. The carter went round the back with the horse, and his mate, the one in the red cap, took a little pot of paste out of his coat and stuck an old label on it, quick as you like. Thought he was fixing it. He looked very pleased with himself.”

file.label: Report to Captain Carrot
file.title: Reporting the sack
file.prompt: “So which tag was right, and how did the other one get there?”
file.reject: Carrot reads your notes carefully. “I don’t think that follows from what you found. Have another look?”

findings.label: The Post Office put the wrong tag on the sack
findings.reject: “The Post Office stamp is pressed over the routing tag,” says Carrot gently, “and the other label is stuck on top of the stamp. That label went on after the sack left them. It wouldn’t be fair to blame the Post Office.”

findings.label: The sack was for the Bonded warehouse; the old label was added after dispatch
findings.summary: Routing tag confirmed; the return label went on after dispatch; nobody named.
findings.reply: “The stamp, the bond book and the tag all agree,” says Carrot. “So the sack goes to the Bonded warehouse, and the old label was added somewhere between here and there. I’ll file it as a routing error. Nobody’s blamed, because we can’t say who did it. That’s fair.”
findings.reject: “You’ll want the Post Office’s side and the warehouse’s side,” says Carrot. “Then we know where it was meant to go, and when the other label went on.”

findings.label: The carter’s mate pasted the old label on at the quay; the sack is held unopened
findings.summary: Old label pasted on at the quay by the carter’s mate; sack held unopened under witness; Post Office cleared.
findings.reply: “A witness, the stamp, the bond book, and the sack still sealed in the quay office,” says Carrot, beaming. “That’s exactly how it should be done. I’ll have a quiet word with the carter’s mate. It may be he thought he was helping. If he wasn’t, we’ll know soon enough, and the sack goes where it belongs either way.”
findings.reject: “For that I need the sack kept safe where it was found, with a witness, and someone who saw the label go on,” says Carrot. “Otherwise it’s just a good guess, and good guesses aren’t evidence.”

cases.title: The Missing Bell
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Temple of Small Gods has lost a bell. Not a small one, either, which you’d think would be the point. There’s a bit of green velvet under the belfry and cart tracks in the mud. Have a look before somebody starts shouting about miracles.”
cases.brief: Find out where the bell went and how. Report only what you can show.

clues.ringer: The bell-ringer says the bell was sold to a scrap dealer as unwanted metal. Who authorised the sale is not known.
clues.dealer: The cart tracks lead to a dealer who has the bell. He bought it as unwanted metal and kept the seller’s details.

scenes.label: Question the bell-ringer
scenes.hint: The person who rings it may know where it went.
scenes.title: The bell-ringer
scenes.speaker: The bell-ringer
scenes.text: “Sold, it was. Somebody said it was cracked and unwanted, and a dealer took it away for the metal. I just ring the things. I don’t sign for them.” He does not know who authorised the sale.

scenes.label: Follow the muddy cart tracks
scenes.hint: See where the cart went.
scenes.title: A bell among the scrap
scenes.speaker: The dealer
scenes.text: The tracks end behind the Shades second-hand counter. The bell is there, upside down, keeping the rain off a crate of spoons. “Bought it fair, as unwanted metal. I wrote down who sold it me. Somewhere.”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Missing Bell
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: The scrap dealer stole the bell
findings.reject: “He bought it and wrote down who from,” says Colon. “That’s a dealer with a receipt, not a thief. Who sold it, though: that’s a question.”

findings.label: The bell was sold as scrap (one account only)
findings.summary: Bell reported sold as scrap; not yet corroborated.
findings.reply: “Sold as scrap. Right, that’s a start,” says Colon. “Next time get both ends of it. Temples get funny about bells.”

findings.label: Sold as unwanted metal: the bell is at the dealer’s and can go back
findings.summary: Bell found at the dealer’s; the sale is recorded; who authorised it goes to the temple.
findings.reply: “Bell found, sale written down, and the temple can work out who sold their own bell,” says Colon. “Nobody arrested and everything back where it was. That’s the dream.”

cases.title: A Pie of Questionable Origin
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Pies going missing off a stall by the Market Hall. Nobody’s seen the thief. Now, I’ve eaten from that stall, and I’m not saying the pies want to escape, but I’m not ruling it out.”
cases.brief: Find out what is taking the pies. Don’t name a thief you haven’t seen.

clues.decoy: A stray dog took the decoy pie to a hiding place under the stall.
clues.tins: Under the stall: a stray dog’s nest and a pile of empty pie tins.

scenes.label: Set a decoy pie
scenes.hint: Leave temptation out and watch.
scenes.title: A decoy pie
scenes.text: You set a pie on the corner of the stall and step back. After a while a thin, determined stray dog emerges, takes the pie with great dignity and carries it under the stall.

scenes.label: Look beneath the stall
scenes.hint: Where would a thief eat?
scenes.title: Beneath the stall
scenes.text: Under the stall you find sacking, a sleepy stray dog and a heap of pie tins licked so clean they could go back on sale. The trader admits that one or two of them have.

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: A Pie of Questionable Origin
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: A rival trader is stealing the pies
findings.reject: “You’ve not seen a trader,” says Colon. “You’ve seen a dog. Dogs don’t have rivals. They have dinner.”

findings.label: Something under the stall is taking them: secure the food
findings.summary: Pies taken from under the stall; culprit not seen.
findings.reply: “Well, it’s not the pies escaping, then,” says Colon. “Tell the trader to put a lid on it.”

findings.label: A stray dog, no human thief: the trader secures the food
findings.summary: A hungry stray dog; the trader will secure the food.
findings.reply: “A dog,” says Colon, deeply relieved. “I’ll tell the trader to put a lid on it. And possibly on the dog.”

cases.title: The Forged Permit
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Night cart up by the Guild Archives with a city permit that looks a bit… artistic. Driver says a clerk gave it him. Nobody’s checked the issuing book.”
cases.brief: Record what can be checked. An odd seal is a reason to look, not proof of forgery.

clues.seal: You copied the unusual seal and the permit reference for the issuing office to check.
clues.clerk: The driver named the clerk who supplied the permit.

scenes.label: Record the seal for verification
scenes.hint: What exactly does the permit say?
scenes.title: The seal
scenes.text: The seal is pressed slightly crooked and the wax is the wrong red, although you are aware that you have no idea what the right red is. You copy the impression and the permit reference carefully.

scenes.label: Ask for the issuing clerk
scenes.hint: Where did the driver get it?
scenes.title: The driver
scenes.speaker: The driver
scenes.text: “Clerk at the office gave it me. Paid the fee and everything.” He names the clerk, then adds hopefully: “Is that bad for him or bad for me?”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Forged Permit
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: The driver forged it: arrest him
findings.reject: “He paid a fee and told you who took it,” says Colon. “Forgers don’t usually volunteer that. Check before you nick.”

findings.label: The permit goes to the issuing office for checking
findings.summary: Permit referred to the issuing office.
findings.reply: “Fair enough. If the office says it’s wrong, we’ll know more,” says Colon.

findings.label: Seal and supplying clerk referred to the issuing office
findings.summary: Seal copied and supplying clerk named for the issuing office to check.
findings.reply: “Seal copied, clerk named, office asked,” says Colon. “If it’s forged, we know who to ask. If it isn’t, nobody’s been embarrassed. Mostly us.”

cases.title: Lights on the River
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Blue lights on the river after midnight, out past the docks. Half the quay thinks it’s ghosts, the other half thinks it’s the first half. A river worker says there’s a line out near the channel.”
cases.brief: Find out what the lights are and whether boats are in danger.

clues.lights: The lights are lanterns on an unattended salvage rig beside the navigation channel.
clues.worker: A river worker identified the rig’s owner and will warn passing boats.

scenes.label: Follow the lights
scenes.hint: Get close enough to see what they hang from.
scenes.title: Blue lights
scenes.text: From the end of the quay the lights resolve into three blue-glassed lanterns on a salvage rig, bobbing beside the navigation channel. Nobody is aboard. Several things are tied to the rig that probably shouldn’t be.

scenes.label: Interview the river worker
scenes.hint: Someone who works the river will know.
scenes.title: The river worker
scenes.speaker: A river worker
scenes.text: “Salvage rig. Blue glass so the fish don’t notice, apparently. Owner leaves it out all night, and one day a barge’ll find it the hard way.” She knows the owner’s mark and offers to warn boats coming through.

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: Lights on the River
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: Ghost lights: nothing to be done
findings.reject: “Ghosts don’t need lanterns,” says Colon. “Well. Most don’t. Something’s floating out there, and boats can hit it.”

findings.label: An unattended rig in the channel
findings.summary: An unattended rig near the channel; owner not yet traced.
findings.reply: “A rig, not a ghost,” says Colon. “Somebody had better warn the boats.”

findings.label: Unattended salvage rig: boats warned, owner being contacted
findings.summary: Salvage rig found; boats warned; owner being contacted.
findings.reply: “Rig found, boats warned, owner on the list,” says Colon. “And no ghosts. I’ll tell the quay. They’ll be disappointed.”

cases.title: The Unpaid Watchman
cases.giverLine: Captain Carrot: “A doorman in the Shades says his employer stopped paying him after he reported a break-in. He isn’t one of ours, but he did the right thing reporting it, and he has asked us to write down what he says.”
cases.brief: Record his account and what can be checked. His employer hasn’t been heard yet.

clues.statement: The doorman reported a break-in, and says his wages stopped afterwards.
clues.wagebook: The wage book shows three payments marked outstanding, all after the break-in report.

scenes.label: Take a witness statement
scenes.hint: Hear it from him, in order.
scenes.title: The doorman
scenes.speaker: The doorman
scenes.text: “I saw them go in the back, I reported it, proper like, and next payday there was nothing. Nor the one after. I’m not asking for trouble. I’m asking for my wages.”

scenes.label: Review the wage book
scenes.hint: What does the employer’s own book say?
scenes.title: The wage book
scenes.text: The landlord’s clerk lets you see the wage book with the air of someone who hopes you can’t read. Three payments to the doorman are marked outstanding, every one of them after the night of the break-in.

file.label: Report to Captain Carrot
file.title: Reporting: The Unpaid Watchman
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Carrot shakes his head gently. “Your notes don’t say that yet. What do you actually know?”

findings.label: His employer is punishing him: charge the employer
findings.reject: “We haven’t heard the employer yet,” says Carrot gently. “Wages and break-ins are both real problems. Neither is a charge until both sides are heard.”

findings.label: His account recorded; the pay dispute referred
findings.summary: Doorman’s account recorded; pay dispute referred.
findings.reply: “Written down properly, and passed on,” says Carrot. “That’s what he asked for.”

findings.label: His word and the wage book: unpaid wages referred with the break-in report
findings.summary: Unpaid wages documented and referred with the break-in report.
findings.reply: “His word and the employer’s own book,” says Carrot. “That goes to the review with the break-in report. He’ll be heard properly now.”

cases.title: The Clock That Struck Thirteen
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Lady up by the Old Crypt says her clock struck thirteen. Wants to know if it’s an omen. I said probably not, but I’d send someone who’s good with omens. That’s you.”
cases.brief: Find out why it strikes thirteen. Don’t call it sabotage without proof.

clues.pin: A displaced pin sits beside the striking wheel.
clues.chime: On the hour, the striking wheel caught and struck a thirteenth time.

scenes.label: Inspect the mechanism
scenes.hint: Open it up.
scenes.title: Behind the dial
scenes.text: Behind the dial, among the gears, a pin has worked loose from its proper hole and sits where the striking wheel brushes past it.

scenes.label: Observe the striking wheel
scenes.hint: Wait for the hour and watch it happen.
scenes.title: On the hour
scenes.text: You wait for the hour with the owner, who offers tea and a running commentary on omens. At the twelfth strike the wheel catches, hesitates and strikes a thirteenth. The owner looks at you as though you did it.

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Clock That Struck Thirteen
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: Someone sabotaged the clock
findings.reject: “A loose pin’s not a crime,” says Colon. “Unless you’ve got someone with a screwdriver and a grudge, it’s just a clock having a bad day.”

findings.label: A fault in the clock: clockmaker requested
findings.summary: A fault in the striking; clockmaker requested.
findings.reply: “Not an omen, then,” says Colon. “I’ll tell her to get it seen to.”

findings.label: Fault seen and explained: a displaced pin, no culprit
findings.summary: A displaced pin catches the striking wheel; clockmaker requested; no culprit.
findings.reply: “Seen it, found it, explained it,” says Colon. “No omen, no saboteur, just a pin. I’ll tell her it’s not the end of the world. She’ll be relieved. Or annoyed.”

cases.title: The Bookseller’s Secret
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “The Lantern & Quill, by the University. Somebody’s been leaving little notes in the damaged books. Unsigned. The owner wants to know who. I said books aren’t really a Watch matter. He said it’s a mystery, and those are.”
cases.brief: Find out who is leaving the notes, and why.

clues.hand: The apprentice recognised the handwriting: the notes warn readers about loose pages.
clues.seen: You saw the apprentice leave a note in a book with a loose binding.

scenes.label: Compare the handwriting
scenes.hint: Whose hand matches?
scenes.title: The handwriting
scenes.speaker: The apprentice
scenes.text: You set one of the notes beside the shop’s order book. The apprentice goes pink. “That’s mine. They’re warnings. ‘Mind the pages, they come out.’ I didn’t want anyone blaming the shop.”

scenes.label: Watch the bookshop door
scenes.hint: Catch the next note being left.
scenes.title: Watching the door
scenes.text: You loiter near the door, which in a bookshop takes no effort at all. Before long the apprentice slides a slip of paper into a book whose spine has given up, glances round, and sees you seeing them.

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Bookseller’s Secret
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: Someone is vandalising the books
findings.reject: “Vandals don’t leave helpful notes,” says Colon. “I’ve met vandals. Their spelling’s worse, for a start.”

findings.label: The apprentice is leaving the notes
findings.summary: The apprentice left the notes; reason not checked.
findings.reply: “Mystery solved, more or less,” says Colon. “Did you ask why?”

findings.label: The apprentice’s warnings about loose pages: the bookseller checks the books
findings.summary: Notes were the apprentice’s warnings; the bookseller will check the books.
findings.reply: “Mystery solved, and the shop’s better for it,” says Colon. “The kid should get a raise. Don’t tell the bookseller I said that.”

cases.title: The Lost Watch Badge
cases.giverLine: Captain Carrot: “Someone found an old Watch badge in the gutter by the Opera House. The number is nearly worn away. Before anyone claims it, we should know whose it was.”
cases.brief: Identify the badge properly. Holding a badge doesn’t make someone its owner.

clues.number: Cleaned, the badge shows enough of its number for a records check.
clues.records: The records match the badge to an officer who reported it lost.

scenes.label: Read the worn badge number
scenes.hint: Clean it and look closely.
scenes.title: A badge in the gutter
scenes.text: In the gutter outside the Opera House lies a badge so worn it could almost be a coin. You polish it on your sleeve until enough of the number shows for the records.

scenes.label: Check the duty records
scenes.hint: The desk keeps every badge number.
scenes.title: The duty records
scenes.speaker: The desk officer
scenes.text: “Badge numbers, badge numbers…” The desk officer runs a finger down a ledger older than some of the constables. “There. Reported lost, years ago. The officer’s still on the books.”

file.label: Report to Captain Carrot
file.title: Reporting: The Lost Watch Badge
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Carrot shakes his head gently. “Your notes don’t say that yet. What do you actually know?”

findings.label: Give it to the first person who claims it
findings.reject: “Anyone can say a badge is theirs,” says Carrot. “That’s rather the problem with badges.”

findings.label: Badge handed to the desk for an identity check
findings.summary: Badge left at the desk for an identity check.
findings.reply: “Good. It’s safe at the desk until we know whose it is,” says Carrot.

findings.label: Badge matched to the officer who lost it; held at the desk for return
findings.summary: Badge matched to its officer and held at the desk for return.
findings.reply: “Matched to the record and kept safe until the owner comes,” says Carrot. “That’s exactly how it should be done.”

cases.title: The Disappearing Door
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Crooked Alley in the Shades. People say there’s a door that moves after dark. Now, in the Shades, things moving after dark is just Tuesday, but this one keeps blocking the alley.”
cases.brief: Find out what the door is, and get the alley clear.

clues.hinges: The ‘door’ is a hinged scenery panel, painted like a door.
clues.porter: The night porter says the panel belongs to a theatrical troupe who rehearse at night.

scenes.label: Inspect the hinges
scenes.hint: Doors that move leave marks.
scenes.title: The hinges
scenes.text: The door is painted on canvas stretched over a frame, and the frame swings on hinges screwed into the wall. Close up, it is a very good door. It is not, however, a door.

scenes.label: Speak to the night porter
scenes.hint: Who’s about at night?
scenes.title: The night porter
scenes.speaker: The night porter
scenes.text: “That? That’s the players’ door. They rehearse at night and swing it out for the scene. Swing it back, mostly. Sometimes they forget, and people walk into the alley and out again looking puzzled.”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Disappearing Door
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: A burglar is using a fake door: lie in wait
findings.reject: “Burglars don’t generally paint their own doors,” says Colon. “Well, there was that one. But he was very bad at it.”

findings.label: A movable panel is blocking the alley
findings.summary: A movable panel blocks the alley; owner not traced.
findings.reply: “A door that isn’t a door,” says Colon. “Whose is it, though?”

findings.label: The troupe’s scenery panel: they keep the alley clear
findings.summary: The troupe’s scenery panel; they will keep the alley clear.
findings.reply: “A door that’s not a door, owned by people pretending to be other people,” says Colon. “Only in the Shades. Alley clear, nobody nicked. Lovely.”

cases.title: A Very Expensive Fish
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Fishmonger at the quay says someone’s had away an enormous fish. Very expensive, apparently. I asked how expensive and he cried. Cart ruts head off towards some banquet.”
cases.brief: Find the fish and how it got there. A debt claim doesn’t settle whose fish it is.

clues.hold: The cart ruts lead to the banquet stores, where a very large fish is in the cool hold.
clues.crews: The crews carried the fish to the banquet on someone’s claim that the fishmonger owed him.

scenes.label: Follow the cart ruts
scenes.hint: Where does a fish that size go?
scenes.title: The cool hold
scenes.text: The ruts lead to the back of the Musicians’ Guild, where a banquet is being prepared on a heroic scale. In the cool hold, under a sheet, is a fish roughly the size of a cellist.

scenes.label: Question the boat crews
scenes.hint: Somebody carried it.
scenes.title: The boat crews
scenes.speaker: A boat hand
scenes.text: “Took it up on the handcart, didn’t we. Bloke said the fishmonger owed him and the fish squared it.” He looks shifty. “Is that not how debts work?”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: A Very Expensive Fish
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: The banquet hosts stole the fish
findings.reject: “They’ve got a fish in a cold room,” says Colon. “That makes them cooks, not crooks. Find out who sent it.”

findings.label: The fish went to the banquet stores
findings.summary: Fish traced to the banquet; how it got there not settled.
findings.reply: “Found the fish, at least,” says Colon. “The fishmonger will want to know who sent it.”

findings.label: Taken over a disputed debt: delivery recorded, the fishmonger to identify it
findings.summary: Fish traced; taken over a disputed debt; ownership to be confirmed.
findings.reply: “Found, traced, and the debt business goes to someone who likes paperwork,” says Colon. “The fishmonger can stop crying. Probably.”

cases.title: The Night-Soil Dispute
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Two businesses by the Market Hall are blaming each other for a pile of… well. Refuse. Both say the same contractor was due to shift it. I said I’d send someone. I didn’t say I’d send someone who wanted to go.”
cases.brief: Find out why the refuse wasn’t collected. Nobody is responsible until the records say so.

clues.route: The contractor’s cart was at its own yard, not at the Market Hall where it was booked.
clues.receipts: Both businesses hold receipts naming the same contractor and collection date.

scenes.label: Follow the cart tracks
scenes.hint: Where did the collection cart actually go?
scenes.title: The collection yard
scenes.text: The cart marks, which are unmistakable in several senses, lead to a collection yard by the Butchers’ Guild. The contractor’s cart is there, not at the Market Hall, where it was booked to be.

scenes.label: Compare collection receipts
scenes.hint: What did each business pay for?
scenes.title: Two receipts
scenes.text: Both shopkeepers produce receipts with the air of people playing a winning card. The receipts name the same contractor, the same date and the same pile. Neither is pleased to find they agree.

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Night-Soil Dispute
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: One of the businesses dumped it
findings.reject: “Both of them paid to have it taken,” says Colon. “Somebody didn’t take it. That’s not the same as somebody dumping it.”

findings.label: A missed collection: clean-up requested
findings.summary: Missed collection; clean-up requested.
findings.reply: “Clean-up requested. I’ll hold my nose and sign it,” says Colon.

findings.label: The contractor missed a paid collection: records requested, clean-up arranged
findings.summary: Contractor missed a booked, paid collection; records requested; clean-up arranged.
findings.reply: “Contractor booked, paid, and somewhere else,” says Colon. “He gets a letter. The street gets cleaned. And I never mention this case again.”

cases.title: The Phantom Watchman
cases.giverLine: Captain Carrot: “Someone in an old Watch uniform walks the corner by the Watch Outpost every night. The duty sheet has nobody there. People are starting to ask him for help, and he isn’t one of us.”
cases.brief: Find out who it is. People mistaking him for an officer could get someone hurt.

clues.roster: The badge number he wears has no current assignment.
clues.observed: He is a delivery runner who wears an old uniform to feel safer.

scenes.label: Check the badge against the roster
scenes.hint: Is that number on duty?
scenes.title: The roster
scenes.speaker: The desk officer
scenes.text: “That number? Not on any sheet this year. Or last year.” The desk officer frowns. “Whoever it is, they’re not on my roster, and I don’t like people who aren’t on my roster.”

scenes.label: Observe the next patrol
scenes.hint: Watch where he actually goes.
scenes.title: The phantom’s round
scenes.text: At the usual time a figure in an old Watch coat appears by the outpost. Instead of walking a beat he follows a route: a door, a parcel, another door. He is a delivery runner. When he catches your eye he looks mortified. “It’s the coat. Nobody bothers you in the coat.”

file.label: Report to Captain Carrot
file.title: Reporting: The Phantom Watchman
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Carrot shakes his head gently. “Your notes don’t say that yet. What do you actually know?”

findings.label: Impersonating an officer: arrest him
findings.reject: “He hasn’t claimed any authority,” says Carrot. “He’s frightened, not wicked. We talk to him before we arrest him.”

findings.label: Not a Watch officer: the number is unassigned
findings.summary: Not a Watch officer; who he is not yet known.
findings.reply: “So he isn’t ours,” says Carrot. “Then who is he, and why the coat?”

findings.label: A runner in an old uniform: warned of the danger, safety concern recorded
findings.summary: A delivery runner in an old uniform; warned; safety concern recorded.
findings.reply: “He gets to deliver his parcels safely, and people stop asking him to arrest their neighbours,” says Carrot. “And I’ll see about a lamp on that corner.”

cases.title: An Unfortunate Portrait
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Somebody’s painted a moustache, and other features, on a portrait at the Lawyers’ Guild. They’re calling it treason against good taste. An apprentice painter has also lodged a complaint about not being paid. Funny, that.”
cases.brief: Find out who altered the portrait and why. The damage and the pay complaint are separate matters.

clues.paint: The paint on the portrait was bought by the apprentice who painted it.
clues.account: The apprentice admits altering the portrait in protest at unpaid work.

scenes.label: Inspect the paint supply
scenes.hint: Who bought that particular colour?
scenes.title: The pigment book
scenes.speaker: The pigment seller
scenes.text: “Bilious green? Only sold one pot of that this month, thank goodness.” The supplier’s book shows it went to the apprentice who painted the guild’s portrait in the first place.

scenes.label: Hear the apprentice’s account
scenes.hint: Let the apprentice speak.
scenes.title: The apprentice
scenes.speaker: The apprentice
scenes.text: “I painted that portrait. Six weeks, and not a penny. So I gave him a moustache. And a squint. And possibly a second chin.” A pause. “Was that wrong?”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: An Unfortunate Portrait
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: Treason against good taste: uphold the guild, dismiss the pay complaint
findings.reject: “Painting a moustache on a lawyer isn’t treason,” says Colon. “Tempting, but not treason. And his pay complaint stands on its own.”

findings.label: The apprentice altered the portrait
findings.summary: The apprentice altered the portrait; pay complaint not looked at.
findings.reply: “Well, that’s who,” says Colon. “There’s still the matter of his wages.”

findings.label: Damage admitted and the pay complaint recorded separately: a hearing for both
findings.summary: Damage admitted; pay complaint recorded separately; hearing requested.
findings.reply: “Damage owned up to, pay complaint written down, both to a hearing,” says Colon. “Fair to everyone. Including the moustache.”

cases.title: The Lantern Tax
cases.giverLine: Sergeant Colon: “Lantern Row. Folk are being charged for a streetlight that hasn’t lit for weeks. Lantern Row, no lantern. You couldn’t make it up. Somebody did, though.”
cases.brief: Find out what has been charged, and why. Who authorised the charge still needs checking.

clues.ledger: The ledger records charges throughout the weeks the lamp was out.
clues.collector: The collector blames a subcontractor who said the repair was done.

scenes.label: Inspect the lighting ledger
scenes.hint: What has been charged, and when?
scenes.title: The lighting ledger
scenes.text: The lighting ledger is kept in a hut at the end of the row. Charges for the lamp continue week after week, straight through the dates the residents say it was dark.

scenes.label: Record the collector’s account
scenes.hint: Hear the man who takes the money.
scenes.title: The collector
scenes.speaker: The collector
scenes.text: “Not my fault. The repair’s subcontracted. Bloke said it was done. Charges go on until somebody says it isn’t done.” He looks up at the dark lamp. “I suppose somebody’s saying it now.”

file.label: Report to Sergeant Colon
file.title: Reporting: The Lantern Tax
file.prompt: “Go on, then. What have you actually got?”
file.reject: Colon squints at your notes. “That’s not what this says, is it? Have another look.”

findings.label: The collector is pocketing the money: arrest him
findings.reject: “Charging for a broken lamp is wrong, but it isn’t the same as stealing,” says Colon. “Who said he could charge? That’s the question.”

findings.label: Charges during an outage: complaint attached, repair requested
findings.summary: Charges during the outage recorded; repair requested.
findings.reply: “Repair requested. With any luck they’ll see their way,” says Colon. “Ha. See their way. Because it’s dark.”

findings.label: Charged for a dark lamp: repair requested, payments referred for review
findings.summary: Charges during the outage; repair requested; payments referred for review.
findings.reply: “Repair asked for, money questions sent up the line,” says Colon. “And Lantern Row might get its lantern. Imagine.”

cases.title: The Thirteenth Chime
cases.giverLine: Captain Carrot: “Every night a bell rings thirteen times. The guild calls it sabotage, a street prophet calls it the end of the world, and the bell-ringer has left his post and come to us. I’d like this one done properly.”
cases.brief: Find the physical clues, take both witnesses’ statements, and report only what the evidence shows. This is a longer case.

clues.shavings: Brass shavings in the bell tower: freshly filed. Someone worked on the bell mechanism from inside.
clues.docket: A midnight delivery docket: a cart of clockwork tools was signed out shortly before the thirteenth chime.
clues.maker: A stallholder recognised the tool mark as one used by a local clockwork workshop.
clues.wheel: An altered timing wheel, hidden in a Shades workshop. Its extra tooth forces thirteen strikes where twelve should sound.
clues.ringer: The bell-ringer heard a click behind the dial before the extra strike: machinery, not footsteps.
clues.clockmaker: The clockmaker says he was hired to repair a faulty mechanism and given the wrong drawings.
clues.mechanism: The thirteenth strike is mechanical: an altered wheel, with tools delivered just before it began.

scenes.label: Search the bell tower
scenes.hint: Start where the bell is.
scenes.title: The bell tower
scenes.text: A thin brass shaving catches the lamplight on the tower stair. The metal is freshly filed. Someone has been working on the bell mechanism from inside.

scenes.label: Check the dock ledger
scenes.hint: Tools have to arrive somehow.
scenes.title: The dock ledger
scenes.text: A delivery receipt bears an oddly precise time. A cart of clockwork tools was signed out shortly before the first thirteenth chime.

scenes.label: Ask at the market stall
scenes.hint: Someone may know the maker’s mark.
scenes.title: The market stall
scenes.speaker: A stallholder
scenes.text: An anxious stallholder turns the tool over and recognises the maker’s mark. “That’s from a clockwork workshop down the Shades. Rents its tools out, too. Check who had them.”

scenes.label: Search the Shades workshop
scenes.hint: The stallholder named a workshop.
scenes.title: The Shades workshop
scenes.text: A loose floorboard conceals a tiny timing wheel. It has one tooth more than it should, which is exactly enough to make twelve into thirteen.

scenes.label: Question the bell-ringer
scenes.hint: He came to the Watch himself.
scenes.title: Witness: the bell-ringer
scenes.speaker: The bell-ringer
scenes.text: “There was a click behind the dial. Then it struck thirteen. I ran because I thought someone had booby-trapped it. I didn’t steal a thing.”

scenes.label: Question the clockmaker
scenes.hint: The workshop has an owner.
scenes.title: Witness: the clockmaker
scenes.speaker: The clockmaker
scenes.text: “I was hired to put right a broken mechanism. Whoever signed the work order gave me the wrong drawings. I can prove it.”

file.label: Present your report to Captain Carrot
file.title: The Thirteenth Chime: your report
file.prompt: “The wheel and the docket suggest someone paid for a change to the bell. They don’t say who, or why. What goes in the report?”
file.reject: Carrot shakes his head gently. “Your notes don’t say that yet. What do you actually know?”

findings.label: Arrest the bell-ringer
findings.reject: “Nothing you’ve found puts the bell-ringer in that workshop,” says Carrot. “He heard machinery and came to us. That isn’t what a saboteur does.”

findings.label: Charge the clockmaker
findings.reject: “A tool mark shows whose tools, not whose idea,” says Carrot. “Check the work order and the drawings before anyone is charged.”

findings.label: The extra strike is mechanical: an altered wheel, delivered at midnight
findings.summary: Extra strike explained as an altered wheel; who ordered it not traced.
findings.reply: “That explains the thirteenth strike,” says Carrot. “It doesn’t explain who wanted it. Good work, but somebody still has to finish this.”

findings.label: Trace the disputed work order before naming anyone
findings.summary: Every clue and both witnesses; the disputed work order is to be traced before anyone is named.
findings.reply: “Every clue, both witnesses, and a recommendation that doesn’t outrun them,” says Carrot. “Whoever signed that work order has some explaining to do, and now we know where to ask.”
